author: Chad Vaughn STAFF WRITER
title: Handley, Sang square off in Mason County Commission race | Gallipolis, Pomeroy, Point Pleasant and Mason News | wvnews.com
text:
POINT PLEASANT, W.Va. — Mason County voters will choose between incumbent Commissioner Rick Handley and local business owner John Bradley “Brad” Sang on the Nov. 3 ballot in the only contested race at the county level.
Handley is seeking reelection with economic development, local oversight of major projects and infrastructure among the issues he says will remain priorities over the next six years, while Sang is calling for stronger development oversight, improved infrastructure, long-term planning and greater transparency in county government.
Both candidates pointed to the rapid pace of development in Mason County and concerns surrounding data centers as major issues facing the next commission.
Handley said Mason County should remain open to responsible economic development while ensuring residents and local leaders have a voice in projects that could affect their communities.
“Mason County should welcome responsible economic development,” Handley said. “I do recognize, as President Trump has stressed multiple times, that data centers can bring significant investment, construction jobs, permanent employment and opportunities for local businesses. However, economic development should not come at the expense of local control or the quality of life of the people who live here.”
Handley said county leaders and residents should know what is being proposed and what effects projects could have on water, electricity, roads, the environment, noise and surrounding property owners.
He said the County Commission should be involved from the beginning through advance notification, public input and reviews of infrastructure and environmental impacts. Handley also said developers should bear costs directly associated with infrastructure improvements required by their projects.
“There should be clear standards for noise, lighting, water usage and other impacts, along with transparency and accountability for commitments made by developers,” Handley said.
Sang said the data center debate has highlighted broader questions about Mason County’s ability to regulate growth and prepare for large-scale development.
While House Bill 2014 has drawn criticism over restrictions on local authority concerning certain developments, Sang questioned whether Mason County had sufficient regulations before the legislation was approved.
“We have been and are still ‘sitting ducks’ waiting to be taken advantage of by large corporations,” Sang said. “We need to act now and develop zoning regulations, if for nothing else to help the commission gain information by future developers.”
Sang said stronger regulations would give county officials more information about proposed projects and help them communicate developers’ plans to residents. He also proposed creating a county engineer position to review construction and land development plans, permitting requirements and tax obligations.
“This prior knowledge would again allow the commission to convey information to the citizens of future developments,” Sang said.
Economic development beyond data centers also remains a priority for both candidates.
Handley said Mason County should pursue a diverse economy focused on long-term employment opportunities including manufacturing, small business, agriculture, tourism, outdoor recreation and industries positioned to benefit from the county’s location along the Ohio River.
He pointed to Nucor as an example of the type of employer capable of creating careers that allow younger residents to remain in Mason County.
Handley said cooperation between the commission, state officials, the Mason County Economic Development Authority, utilities and schools will be necessary to ensure businesses have the infrastructure and workers they need.
“Workforce development is especially important,” Handley said. “The Mason County Career Center is doing an excellent job of working with local employers to train people for the jobs that actually exist here.”
Sang likewise called for stronger communication among state, county and local officials. He said Mason County should use its economic development agency to pursue retail businesses, restaurants, hotels, resorts and light manufacturing while seeking industries that complement existing development.
“We need to look more globally for long-lasting future developments,” Sang said. “What is the world going to need that we as county may be able to offer long term.”
Sang also proposed forming an advisory council consisting of residents from different age groups, income levels, backgrounds and areas of the county to provide additional perspectives on development decisions.
Infrastructure emerged as another shared concern.
“The single biggest issue facing Mason County over the next six years is infrastructure, and that includes housing,” Handley said. “If we want to attract new businesses, create jobs and bring new families into the county, we have to have the roads, water and sewer systems, utilities and housing needed to support that growth.”
Handley said he plans to continue working with the Housing Committee of the Mason County Economic Development Authority to identify developers, available properties and infrastructure barriers while expanding housing options for working families.
For Sang, infrastructure is closely connected to the need for a broader plan for future growth.
“Infrastructure, infrastructure, infrastructure, strategic operational procedures for the county and a road map for future developments are the keys for the next six years,” Sang said.
Sang said Nucor’s arrival demonstrated that Mason County was not fully prepared for the pace of development that could follow. He pointed to available flat land, river access, rail service and the county’s road network as factors making the area increasingly attractive to major companies.
“We need to protect our citizens, our farms and the vast heritage that Mason County has all while growing responsibly,” he said.
Sang also called for making county government more accessible through meeting times convenient for working residents, livestreaming meetings and creating a county website and potentially an app for public information.
Handley emphasized continuing partnerships already underway to address development, infrastructure and housing needs while maintaining local involvement as Mason County grows.
Both candidates will appear on the Nov. 3 ballot, with Handley as the candidate for the Democrats and Sang as a Republican, as voters decide who will hold the commission seat for the next term.
